title: Sacrifice and memorial (CCC 1362–1372)
hookLine: the one sacrifice of Christ made present, not repeated

lines: THE WORDS OF THE LAST SUPPER.
cards: Is the Mass a fresh sacrifice every time? It's a fair question, asked sincerely or as a challenge. At Mass, a priest takes bread and wine and says the words Jesus said at the Last Supper.

If that's a sacrifice, is Christ being offered again and again? The Catechism's answer hangs on one small Greek word in Jesus's command at the Last Supper, and it doesn't mean quite what English means by remember.

teach.h: DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.
teach.b: At the Last Supper, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me."
Commemoration, or memorial. Behind it is the Greek anamnesis. In Scripture, the Catechism says, a memorial isn't only recalling the past.
It proclaims what God has done, and in the liturgy those events become, in a certain way, present and real.
Think of Passover: each time Israel celebrates it, the Exodus is made present to the memory of believers, so they shape their lives by it.
So when the Church keeps the memorial of Christ's Passover, his death and resurrection, that event is made present. The one sacrifice Christ offered once for all on the cross stays present.
That's why the Eucharist is also a sacrifice.
Not because something new happens to Christ, but because it makes present the sacrifice of the cross, is its memorial, and applies its fruit. The Catechism is careful here.

Christ's sacrifice and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice. The victim is one and the same: the Christ who offered himself on the cross now offers, through the ministry of priests.
Only the manner differs: on the cross with blood, at the altar without.

And the Church joins in: the Pope, the bishops and the whole people unite their praise, sufferings and work to his offering, and the saints in heaven join in it too. It's offered for the dead as well.
So the answer to the hook is no.

how: At each Mass the priest repeats Christ's words over the bread and wine; the congregation is invited to offer their own lives with Christ's offering, and Masses are often offered for the dead.

o: a prayer asking God to forget all our sins
a sad, private memory of someone who has died
a memorial that makes a past saving act present

games.q: sacrifice and memorial — tap the pairs.

s: the Catechism teaches that Christ is sacrificed again at each Mass
it says the one sacrifice of the cross is made present, not repeated.
in Scripture, a memorial is more than remembering
it proclaims God's deeds, and in the liturgy they become present and real.
the cross and the Mass are two different sacrifices
the Catechism calls them one single sacrifice; only the manner of offering differs.

games.q: a friend asks: if the Mass is a sacrifice, isn't Christ being offered again and again? how does the Catechism answer?
o: yes, a new sacrifice each time.
no, it's only a reminder, like a photo.
no, the one sacrifice of the cross is made present.
games.why: the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, is its memorial, and applies its fruit: present, not repeated.

practice: Picture the moment in the Mass when the priest repeats the words of the Last Supper and lifts up the host.
Decide what you'd bring to that moment: one worry, one piece of work, one person, one hard thing from this week, since the Catechism says people can unite these to his offering.
If you pray, hold that one thing now, ready to bring; if you don't go to Mass, simply hold it, and notice what it would mean to offer it.

wordCard.voice: Anamnesis. Memorial: not just remembering the past, but making Christ's one sacrifice present in the liturgy. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the memorial word in Jesus's command, do this for a commemoration of me.

carryVoice: Your line: present, not repeated. A memorial that does more than remember. Back tomorrow, same hill.
